Formatting Syntax

Source: vignettes/overview-formatting-syntax.Rmd
overview-formatting-syntax.Rmd

guess_data_type() tells you what a column is. Stabilizing is the other half of formex: taking the raw values and rewriting them into a clean, standard, analysis-ready form — and attaching the rule that lets anyone reopen the file without corrupting it. This is the package’s workhorse data-management functionality, and it is entirely rule-driven: every semantic type in the ontology ships with a pre-set transformation recipe, so cleaning a column is a lookup, not a bespoke script.

This guide explains the stabilizer by example, through a table that recurs throughout:

column what it is
RAW an example value as it arrives in the file
semantic type where guess_data_type() placed it
format observed the pattern the raw value matches, in formex syntax
stabilizer the function the recipe runs
target format what the cleaned value looks like
STABLE the new, standardized value

The one syntax rule: anything inside {{ … }} is parsed by formex; anything outside is a human comment. (The full grammar is the Formex: the format-expression syntax article.) Every “format observed” and “stabilizer” cell below is read live from fx_ontology(), and every STABLE value is the live output of fx_stabilize().

The workflow at a glance

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
03/15/2019 ;; 12/31/2020 calendar {{ mmddyyyy }} {{ as_mmddyyyy }} ISO 8601 date 2019-03-15 ;; 2020-12-31
2,300.00;;17,2982,300.00 ;; 17,298 ;; $-45 |usd |<code>{{ [strip:$,][range:-Inf,Inf][dec:.2] }} {{ as_usd }} numeric (unit: USD) 2300 ;; 17298 ;; -45
California ;; TX ;; Ohio geographic / us_state {{ lexicon:usps_state }} lookup:usps USPS 2-letter CA ;; TX ;; OH
yes ;; 0 ;; t ;; x ;; no mixed {{ tf|yn|10|check blank=false }} {{ as_boolean }} TRUE / FALSE TRUE ;; FALSE ;; TRUE ;; TRUE ;; FALSE
40° 44’ 55” N, 74° 00’ 22” W lat_lon / dms {{ gcs:dms:latlon }} {{ as_coord_latlon }} decimal degrees 40.748611, -74.006111

Read any row left to right: a messy RAW value, matched by a format, run through a stabilizer, lands on a clean STABLE value. The rest of this guide takes the main transformation families one at a time.

Calendar dates: many ways in, one way out

Dates are the canonical case. The same day arrives written a dozen ways; the stabilizer normalizes every one to unambiguous ISO YYYY-MM-DD, so the column is internally consistent and no locale can re-read 03/04 as the wrong day.

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
03/15/2019 ;; 12/31/2020 calendar {{ mmddyyyy }} {{ as_mmddyyyy }} ISO 8601 2019-03-15 ;; 2020-12-31
2019-03-15 ;; 2020-12-31 calendar {{ mmddyyyy }} {{ as_mmddyyyy }} ISO 8601 2019-03-15 ;; 2020-12-31
March 15, 2019 ;; December 31, 2020 calendar {{ mmddyyyy }} {{ as_mmddyyyy }} ISO 8601 2019-03-15 ;; 2020-12-31 
fx_stabilize(c("03/15/2019", "March 15, 2019", "2019-03-15"), "calendar")$stable
#> [1] "2019-03-15" "2019-03-15" "2019-03-15"

The recipe also hands back an import rule — for a date, {{ as_yyyymmdd }} — that tells the next reader to load the clean value back as a true date, not as text. Classification and stabilization speak the same ontology, so the output of one flows straight into the other:

x     <- c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021")
route <- guess_data_type(x)$route
fx_stabilize(x, route$semantic_type)$stable
#> [1] "2019-03-15" "2020-12-31" "2021-01-01"

Date-times and time zones: the zone is a unit

A timestamp is a date plus a clock. The stabilizer normalizes the written form to ISO 8601 (2019-03-15T14:30:00), whatever shape it arrived in:

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
2019-03-15 14:30:00 ;; 2020-12-31 08:05:00 timestamp {{ mmddyyyy hh:ii12A }} {{ as_datetime }} ISO 8601 date-time 2019-03-15T14:30:00 ;; 2020-12-31T08:05:00
3/15/2019 14:30 ;; 12/31/2020 8:05 timestamp {{ mmddyyyy hh:ii12A }} {{ as_datetime }} ISO 8601 date-time 2019-03-15T14:30:00 ;; 2020-12-31T08:05:00 
fx_stabilize(c("2019-03-15 14:30:00", "3/15/2019 14:30"), "timestamp")$stable
#> [1] "2019-03-15T14:30:00" "2019-03-15T14:30:00"

Where does the time zone go? This is exactly what unit_type is for. The timestamp leaf records its unit as datetime; timezone:

o$unit_type[o$semantic_type == "timestamp"]
#> [1] "datetime;;timezone"

Normalizing the format (how the clock is written) and converting the unit (which zone it is in) are two different operations. formex always normalizes the format; a zone conversion — say, rendering a UTC column in US/Eastern — is a unit conversion, the same category of operation as Celsius→Fahrenheit or calendar-year→fiscal-year. Those run through the transform planner (fx_plan_transform()) and fire only when a converter for that unit pair is registered. So the zone is never silently dropped from the model: it is tracked as the unit, ready for a conversion step when one is wired in.

Geographic transformations

Geographies are a closed, table-backed vocabulary, which makes them ideal for rule-driven cleaning: a lookup collapses every spelling to one canonical code, and a coordinate recipe reprojects messy degree notations to decimal degrees.

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
California ;; TX ;; Ohio geographic / us_state {{ lexicon:usps_state }} lookup:usps USPS 2-letter CA ;; TX ;; OH
France ;; FR geographic / iso_country {{ lexicon:iso3166 }} lookup:iso3166 ISO 3166 alpha-2 FR ;; FR
06037 ;; 36061 geographic / county_fips {{ mask:fips5 + lexicon:fips }} {{ as_fips }} 5-digit FIPS 06037 ;; 36061
40° 44’ 55” N, 74° 00’ 22” W lat_lon / dms {{ gcs:dms:latlon }} {{ as_coord_latlon }} decimal degrees (EPSG:4326) 40.748611, -74.006111 
# free-text state names and abbreviations collapse to one canonical code
fx_stabilize(c("California", "TX", "Ohio", "new york"), "geographic", "us_state")$stable
#> [1] "CA" "TX" "OH" "NY"

# a degrees-minutes-seconds pair is reprojected to decimal degrees, latitude first
fx_stabilize("40° 44' 55\" N, 74° 00' 22\" W", "lat_lon", "dms")$stable
#> [1] "40.748611, -74.006111"

Note the county_fips import rule is {{ as_factor }}, and the broader geographic key type hardens a numeric GEOID by prefixing it (FIPS-06037) so no spreadsheet can strip its leading zero. The recipe is selective, too: a value that is not a valid 5-digit county (a stray 4-digit form number, say) stabilizes to NA rather than being force-padded into a bogus code.

Cleaning messy variables

The same machinery tidies the everyday mess of real survey and administrative data.

Currencies strip symbols and grouping marks and return a bare number you can compute on — while the currency itself rides along as the unit_type rather than being buried in the text. European notation (dot-thousands, comma-decimal) is a separate leaf with its own recipe:

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
2,300.00;;17,2982,300.00 ;; 17,298 ;; $-45 |usd |<code>{{ [strip:$,][range:-Inf,Inf][dec:.2] }} {{ as_usd }} numeric (unit: USD) 2300 ;; 17298 ;; -45
2.300,00 € ;; € 45,00 euro {{ [strip:€.][range:-Inf,Inf][dec:,2] }} {{ as_euro }} numeric (unit: EUR) 2300 ;; 45

Mixed-encoding booleans — the classic IRS-990 case where one column holds yes, 0, t, and a bare x — collapse to clean logicals:

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
yes ;; 0 ;; t ;; x ;; no mixed {{ tf|yn|10|check blank=false }} {{ as_boolean }} TRUE / FALSE TRUE ;; FALSE ;; TRUE ;; TRUE ;; FALSE 
fx_stabilize(c("yes", "0", "t", "x", "no"), "mixed")$stable
#> [1] "TRUE"  "FALSE" "TRUE"  "TRUE"  "FALSE"

Ordered categories keep their level order for analysis. The code→label dictionary lives alongside the data; the recipe records that the result is an ordered factor:

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
1 ;; 2 ;; 3 ;; 2 ;; 1 ordered {{ code }} {{ as_ordered }} ordered factor 1 ;; 2 ;; 3 ;; 2 ;; 1

In every case the stabilizer reports what it could not convert rather than failing silently — the conversion_log in the fx_stabilize() return records how many present values were dropped to NA, and why.

Bring your own: a custom stabilizer

The shipped recipes cover the common cases, but a project often needs its own — collapsing a column into house-specific buckets, applying an internal coding scheme. The design is open: a stabilizer is just an R function of the values, and a recipe names it in its stabilizer column. You keep your project’s functions in a small script — call it dg.R — and the recipe refers to them by name.

Say you want to collapse US states into Census regions. The function, as it would live in dg.R:

# --- dg.R : project-specific stabilizers ------------------------------------
as_region <- function(x, a = NA) {
  region <- c(
    CT = "Northeast", ME = "Northeast", MA = "Northeast", NH = "Northeast",
    RI = "Northeast", VT = "Northeast", NJ = "Northeast", NY = "Northeast",
    PA = "Northeast",
    IL = "Midwest", IN = "Midwest", MI = "Midwest", OH = "Midwest",
    WI = "Midwest", IA = "Midwest", KS = "Midwest", MN = "Midwest",
    MO = "Midwest", NE = "Midwest", ND = "Midwest", SD = "Midwest",
    DE = "South", FL = "South", GA = "South", MD = "South", NC = "South",
    SC = "South", VA = "South", DC = "South", WV = "South", AL = "South",
    KY = "South", MS = "South", TN = "South", AR = "South", LA = "South",
    OK = "South", TX = "South",
    AZ = "West", CO = "West", ID = "West", MT = "West", NV = "West",
    NM = "West", UT = "West", WY = "West", AK = "West", CA = "West",
    HI = "West", OR = "West", WA = "West")
  unname(region[toupper(trimws(x))])
}

Once that name is registered in formex’s verb library (assume it is wired in here), an ontology row can reference it in its stabilizer column exactly like a built-in, and the workflow table reads the same as every row above:

RAW semantic type format observed stabilizer target format STABLE
NY ;; CA ;; TX ;; IL geographic / us_region {{ lexicon:usps_state }} {{ as_region }} census_region (factor) Northeast ;; West ;; South ;; Midwest 
# the recipe's stabilizer, applied directly
as_region(c("NY", "CA", "TX", "IL"))
#> [1] "Northeast" "West"      "South"     "Midwest"

That is the whole point of a rule-driven engine: whether a transformation ships with the package or you wrote it this morning, it plugs into the same RAW → format → stabilizer → STABLE pathway, and the resulting file is cleaned and self-describing by the same rules.
